events.title: Indigo revolt (the "Blue Rebellion")
events.summary: In March 1859 thousands of ryots in Bengal refused to grow indigo and fought the planters (NCERT).
events.detail:
European planters forced ryots to grow indigo on their best land through loans that never ended, and paid them very little. Indigo also exhausted the soil (NCERT).

In March 1859 the ryots refused to grow indigo, stopped paying rent to the planters and attacked indigo factories. Women joined with pots and pans; planters' agents were boycotted (NCERT). The government set up the Indigo Commission (1860).
events.place: Nadia, Jessore and other districts of Bengal

sides.name: Indigo ryots
sides.ruler: Village headmen and some zamindars led them (NCERT)

causes: The planters' loan system trapped ryots in endless debt (NCERT).
Planters insisted on the best soils, where ryots wanted rice (NCERT).
Indigo exhausted the soil (NCERT).
The ryots believed the government, worried after 1857, would support them (NCERT).
course: March 1859: thousands of ryots refuse to grow indigo (NCERT).
They attack indigo factories with swords, spears and bows (NCERT).
Planters' agents (gomasthas) are beaten and boycotted (NCERT).
1860: the Indigo Commission hears witnesses such as Hadji Mulla (NCERT).
outcomes: The Indigo Commission held the planters guilty and said ryots could refuse indigo in future (NCERT).
Indigo production collapsed in Bengal; planters moved to Bihar.
Champaran in Bihar (1917) later became the scene of Gandhi's first satyagraha in India (NCERT).
facts: The indigo revolt began in March 1859 in Bengal (NCERT).
The Indigo Commission (1860) declared indigo production not profitable for ryots (NCERT).
Hadji Mulla told the Commission: "I would rather beg than sow indigo" (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: The Indigo Commission is set up; Dinabandhu Mitra writes Nil Darpan.

events.yearHook: Two years after 1857: 1859 — the first big peasant revolt.

participants.role: His play Nil Darpan (1860) told the story of the ryots' suffering.
First Viceroy; his government appointed the Indigo Commission.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"
events.before: European planters forced Bengal peasants to grow indigo at low prices under contracts they could not escape.
events.after: Peasants refused to sow; the **Indigo Commission** (1860) said they could not be forced. Dinabandhu Mitra's play **Nil Darpan** (1860) exposed the planters.
events.today: Champaran (1917) — Gandhi's first satyagraha in India — was also about indigo (the tinkathia system).

events.title: Indian Penal Code
events.summary: The Indian Penal Code, drafted by Macaulay's Law Commission, becomes law.
events.detail: The First Law Commission under Macaulay (1834–38) had drafted a penal code. After the revolt the Crown government passed it in 1860; it came into force in 1862. The Code of Civil Procedure (1859) and Criminal Procedure (1861) followed.
causes: The need for one criminal law for all of British India.
outcomes: The IPC remained India's criminal code until 2024.
events.yearHook: 1860 IPC → 1861 Councils Act and High Courts Act.

participants.role: Drafted the code as head of the First Law Commission.
Viceroy when it was passed.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The first Law Commission under **Macaulay** (1834–37) drafted the code.
events.after: The **CrPC** (1861) and the **Evidence Act** (1872) followed; together they ran Indian criminal law for 160 years.
events.today: They were replaced in July 2024 by the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**, the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam**.

events.title: Indian Councils Act, 1861
events.summary: Indians are nominated to the Viceroy's legislative council for the first time.
events.detail: After 1857 the British wanted to know Indian opinion. The Act added non-official members — some of them Indians — to the Viceroy's council for making laws, and gave back law-making powers to Bombay and Madras. It also gave legal standing to the portfolio system started by Canning. The Indian High Courts Act of the same year led to High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1862).
causes: The revolt showed the danger of ruling without knowing Indian opinion.
course: Non-official members added to the Viceroy's legislative council.
Canning nominated three Indians: the Raja of Benares, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.
Bombay and Madras got back law-making powers (decentralisation).
outcomes: First step in associating Indians with law-making.
High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1862).
facts: Indian Councils Acts: 1861, 1892, 1909.
Canning nominated the Raja of Benares, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.
events.yearHook: Councils Acts every few decades: 1861, 1892, 1909.

participants.role: Viceroy who nominated the first Indian members and started the portfolio system.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: After 1857 the British felt they needed to know Indian opinion.
events.after: A few Indians (the Raja of Benares, the Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao) were nominated; **Canning**'s portfolio system was made legal; provinces got back law-making powers.
events.today: The portfolio system is the root of today's cabinet ministries.
events.mnemonic: Council Acts "61-92-09": 1861 (Indians nominated; portfolio system), 1892 (indirect election; budget discussion), 1909 (separate electorates).

events.title: Kuka (Namdhari) movement
events.summary: Ram Singh's Kuka followers in the Punjab clash with the British; dozens are blown from guns at Malerkotla (1872).
events.detail: The Namdhari or Kuka movement began as a Sikh religious reform movement. Under Ram Singh it preached boycott of British goods, schools and courts. In January 1872 Kukas attacked Malerkotla; the Deputy Commissioner had 65 captured Kukas blown away from guns. Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon.
causes: Religious reform turned into opposition to British rule.
Disputes over cow slaughter in Punjab towns.
outcomes: Crushed by force; the movement continued peacefully.
events.yearHook: 1872: the year Mayo was assassinated and the first census was attempted.

participants.role: Led the movement; exiled to Rangoon.
Viceroy at the time.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: **Bhai Ram Singh** founded the Namdhari (Kuka) sect (1857) in Punjab to purify Sikhism; it boycotted British goods and courts.
events.after: After attacks on butchers (1871–72) the British blew dozens of Kukas from cannons at Malerkotla; Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon.
events.today: The Namdharis are seen as early users of boycott and swadeshi.

events.title: Satyashodhak Samaj and Gulamgiri
events.summary: Jyotirao Phule founds the Satyashodhak Samaj and writes Gulamgiri (1873) against caste oppression (NCERT).
events.detail: Phule argued that the "upper" castes had no right to land and power, and that Shudras and Ati Shudras should unite against caste discrimination (NCERT). His Satyashodhak Samaj ("Society of Truth Seekers") spread caste equality. In 1873 he wrote Gulamgiri (Slavery), linking the condition of the lower castes with that of slaves in America (NCERT).
causes: Caste discrimination against Shudras and Ati Shudras (NCERT).
outcomes: Started the non-Brahmin movement in Maharashtra.
facts: In 1873 Phule wrote Gulamgiri, meaning slavery (NCERT).
Phule dedicated Gulamgiri to the Americans who had fought to free slaves (NCERT).
The first Singh Sabha is formed at Amritsar (NCERT).

Caste movements: Satyashodhak Samaj (Maharashtra) and the Self-Respect agitation (Tamil Nadu); the Ghadar movement and the Bijolia peasant movement (Rajasthan, 1897–1941) were not caste movements (APPSC Group-1 key).
Bahujan Samaj (Satara, 1910) was founded by Mukundrao Patil as an offshoot of the Satyashodhak movement (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

alsoOn.text: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule open a school for girls in Pune.

events.yearHook: 1873 Gulamgiri — ten years after the American Civil War ended slavery (NCERT).

participants.role: Founded the Samaj and wrote Gulamgiri (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 7
events.before: Jyotirao and **Savitribai Phule** had opened a girls' school in Pune (1848) and schools for Dalits.
events.after: The non-Brahmin movement spread in Maharashtra (Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur, reservations 1902) and the Bahujan Samaj (1910). **Ambedkar** called Phule one of his three gurus.
events.today: Savitribai Phule's birthday (3 January) is celebrated as a day for women's education.

events.title: Deccan riots
events.summary: Ryots in the Bombay Deccan attack moneylenders and burn their account books (NCERT Class 12).
events.detail: The ryotwari revenue was high, and when cotton prices crashed after the American Civil War (1865), ryots could not repay loans. Moneylenders refused new credit and took over land. In May 1875 ryots of Supa (Poona district) attacked the shops and houses of moneylenders and burned their account books (bahi khatas) and bonds.
events.place: Supa and other villages of Poona and Ahmednagar
causes: High revenue demand under ryotwari.
The end of the cotton boom (1861–65) after the American Civil War.
Moneylenders refused loans and seized land.
outcomes: The Deccan Riots Commission reported in 1878.
The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) protected peasants from moneylenders.
facts: Ryots in Deccan villages rebelled in 1875 (NCERT Class 12 timeline).
events.yearHook: Cotton boom 1861 → bust 1865 → riots 1875 (NCERT timeline).

participants.role: Viceroy at the time.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 10 "Colonialism and the Countryside"
events.before: Under **ryotwari** peasants borrowed from moneylenders; the American Civil War cotton boom ended (1865) and prices fell.
events.after: Peasants of Poona and Ahmednagar attacked moneylenders and burnt their bonds; the **Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act** (1879) followed.
events.today: An early example of peasants fighting debt; studied with the later Kisan Sabhas.

events.title: MAO College, Aligarh
events.summary: Sayyid Ahmed Khan founds the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (NCERT).
events.detail: The college offered modern education, including Western science, to Muslims, and later became Aligarh Muslim University. The Aligarh Movement had an enormous impact on educational reform (NCERT).
causes: Muslims lagged in English education after 1857.
outcomes: Became Aligarh Muslim University (1920).
facts: The MAO College was founded in 1875 at Aligarh (NCERT).

Muslim movements: Aligarh — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; Faraizi (Bengal) — Haji Shariatullah, then Dudu Miyan; Taiyuni (Taayuni) — Maulvi Karamat Ali Jaunpuri; Deoband (1866) — Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi; Ahmadiyya (1889) — Mirza Ghulam Ahmad; Wahabi (India) — Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: 1875: Arya Samaj and Aligarh — the same year.

participants.role: Founded the college.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 7
events.before: **Sayyid Ahmad Khan** believed Muslims had fallen behind because they shunned Western education after 1857; he founded the **Scientific Society** (1864).
events.after: The MAO College became **Aligarh Muslim University** (1920). Sayyid Ahmad opposed the Congress, which later fed Muslim separatism (Muslim League, 1906).
events.today: AMU's minority status case was decided by the Supreme Court in 2024.

events.title: Great Famine of 1876–78
events.summary: Drought brings one of the worst famines of the century to Madras, Bombay and Mysore; millions die.
events.detail: The monsoon failed in the Deccan and south India. Grain was still exported, relief was kept low to save money, and starving people were made to work on relief camps for little food. Between 5 and 10 million people died. Lytton held the Delhi Durbar in the middle of it.
causes: Failure of the monsoon (1876).
Low relief and continued grain exports.
losses: About 5–10 million people died, mostly in Madras, Bombay, Mysore and Hyderabad.
outcomes: The Famine Commission under Richard Strachey (1878–80) drew up the first Famine Code.
events.yearHook: Famine 1876–78 and the Delhi Durbar 1877 — at the same time.

participants.role: Viceroy; criticised for the Delhi Durbar during the famine and for low relief.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Drought struck the Madras and Bombay Presidencies; the government kept exporting grain.
events.after: About 5 to 10 million died; **Lytton** held the 1877 durbar at the same time. The **Famine Commission** (Strachey, 1880) and the Famine Code followed.
events.today: Rayalaseema and the Deccan districts suffered most; it shaped the drain-of-wealth argument of Naoroji.

events.title: Indian Association of Calcutta
events.summary: Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose found the Indian Association — one of the main associations before the Congress (NCERT).
events.detail: Political associations formed in the 1870s and 1880s, led mostly by English-educated professionals, stated their goals as the goals of all Indians (NCERT). The Indian Association campaigned against lowering the maximum age for the ICS exam (from 21 to 19, 1876) and against the Vernacular Press and Arms Acts.
causes: Need for an all-India political voice.
Lowering of the ICS age limit made it harder for Indians to compete.
outcomes: Held all-India conferences (1883, 1885) and merged into the Congress (1886).
facts: NCERT lists the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, Indian Association, Madras Mahajan Sabha and Bombay Presidency Association as the important early associations.

alsoOn.text: The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha is formed.

events.yearHook: Indian Association 1876 → Congress 1885, nine years later.

participants.role: Co-founded the association and toured India for it.
Viceroy whose policies it opposed.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: **Surendranath Banerjea** had been dismissed from the ICS; the age limit for the exam was cut to 19 (1876).
events.after: The Association ran an all-India campaign on the ICS issue and held a **National Conference** (1883, 1885), which merged into the Congress.
events.today: Banerjea is called "Rashtraguru"; he later accepted the 1919 reforms.
events.mnemonic: Pre-Congress bodies "L-B-E-P-I-M" by year: Landholders' Society (1838), British Indian Association (1851), East India Association (London, 1866, Naoroji), Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), Indian Association (1876, S. N. Banerjea), Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884).

events.title: Delhi Durbar: Victoria proclaimed Empress of India
events.summary: On 1 January 1877 Lytton holds a grand Durbar in Delhi to proclaim Queen Victoria Kaiser-i-Hind.
events.detail: The Royal Titles Act (1876) gave Queen Victoria the title Empress of India. Lytton held a costly Durbar at Delhi to proclaim it before the princes — while famine killed millions in the south. Indian newspapers criticised it bitterly.
causes: Royal Titles Act, 1876.
Wish to bind the princes to the Crown.
outcomes: Strengthened the image of the Raj but angered educated Indians during the famine.

alsoOn.text: Royal Titles Act gives Queen Victoria the title "Empress of India".

events.yearHook: Three Delhi Durbars: 1877 (Victoria), 1903 (Edward VII), 1911 (George V).

participants.role: Organised the Durbar.
Proclaimed Empress of India.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The **Royal Titles Act** (1876) made Victoria "Empress of India" (Kaiser-i-Hind).
events.after: Lytton held the durbar during a terrible famine (1876–78) in the south; Indians were angered. Durbars followed in 1903 (Edward VII) and 1911 (George V, capital to Delhi).
events.today: The Coronation Park in north Delhi was the site of all three durbars.

events.title: Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act
events.summary: Lytton's government passes the Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act to silence critics (NCERT).
events.detail: The Arms Act (1878) disallowed Indians from possessing arms (NCERT). The Vernacular Press Act, the same year, allowed the government to seize the assets of Indian-language newspapers, including their presses, if they published anything "objectionable" (NCERT). English papers were not covered. Amrita Bazar Patrika turned itself into an English paper overnight to escape it.
causes: Indian-language newspapers criticised the famine policy and the Durbar.
course: 1878: Vernacular Press Act passed — the "Gagging Act".
1878: Arms Act — Indians need licences for arms; Europeans exempt.
losses: Indian-language press: freedom to criticise the government.
outcomes: Dissatisfaction with British rule intensified in the 1870s and 1880s (NCERT).
facts: The Arms Act was passed in 1878 (NCERT).
The Vernacular Press Act (1878) let the government confiscate presses of newspapers publishing "objectionable" material (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Press gagged 1878, freed by Ripon 1882.

participants.role: Viceroy whose government passed both Acts.
Repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"
events.before: Indian-language papers criticised the durbar during the famine and the Afghan war.
events.after: The **Vernacular Press Act** (the "gagging act") let officials seize presses of Indian-language papers; the **Amrita Bazar Patrika** turned into an English paper overnight to escape it. **Ripon** repealed it (1882).
events.today: Press freedom debates still cite it; the Indian Arms Act (1878) was replaced by the Arms Act, 1959.

events.title: Second Anglo-Afghan War
events.summary: Lytton invades Afghanistan (1878–80) to keep out Russian influence; the Treaty of Gandamak gives Britain control of Afghan foreign policy.
events.detail: When the Afghan Amir Sher Ali received a Russian mission but refused a British one, Lytton sent troops. The Treaty of Gandamak (1879) made Afghanistan conduct its foreign affairs through Britain. A revolt in Kabul followed; Abdur Rahman became Amir in 1880.

treaties.name: Treaty of Gandamak
terms: Afghan foreign policy to be conducted through Britain.

causes: Fear of Russian influence in Afghanistan.
outcomes: Abdur Rahman became Amir (1880); Britain kept control of Afghan foreign policy.

participants.role: Viceroy who started the war.
Viceroy who ended it (1880).

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: A Russian mission reached Kabul; Lytton followed a "forward policy".
events.after: The **Treaty of Gandamak** (1879) gave Britain control of Afghan foreign policy; a later revolt and Ripon's withdrawal (1880–81) left **Abdur Rahman** as Amir. The **Durand Line** (1893) fixed the border.
events.today: The Durand Line is the disputed Pakistan–Afghanistan border.

events.title: First Factory Act and the first regular census
events.summary: Ripon's government regulates child labour in factories and holds India's first synchronous census.
events.detail: The Factory Act of 1881 banned work by children under 7, limited hours for children under 12, and required fencing of dangerous machines. The same year the first regular census was taken across India at one time.
causes: Lancashire mill-owners complained of "unfair" cheap labour in Indian mills.
outcomes: A second Factory Act followed in 1891 (Lansdowne).
events.yearHook: Census years end in 1: 1881, 1891, 1901, 1911…

participants.role: Viceroy who passed the Act and held the census.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Lancashire mill owners complained that Indian mills used cheap child labour.
events.after: The **Factory Act 1881** banned work by children under 7 and limited hours for children; the 1891 Act extended it. The first synchronous **census** (1881, Plowden) was held.
events.today: Labour codes (2020) replaced the old factory and labour laws.

events.title: Theosophical Society moves to Adyar
events.summary: Blavatsky and Olcott set up the headquarters of the Theosophical Society at Adyar, Madras.
events.detail: Founded in New York in 1875, the Society admired Hindu and Buddhist philosophy. Its Indian headquarters at Adyar became a centre of cultural revival; Annie Besant later led it.
causes: Western interest in Indian spirituality.
outcomes: Gave Indians pride in their own traditions.

alsoOn.text: Helena Blavatsky and Henry Olcott found the Theosophical Society in New York.

events.yearHook: Founded 1875 (the Arya Samaj year), moved to Adyar 1882.

participants.role: Co-founder.
Co-founder and first president.
Joined in 1889 and led it from 1907.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The Theosophical Society was founded in **New York** (1875) by **Madame Blavatsky** and **Colonel Olcott**.
events.after: **Annie Besant** (in India from 1893) founded the **Central Hindu College**, Benares (1898; later BHU, 1916) and the **Home Rule League** (1916).
events.today: The Adyar headquarters (Chennai) still has its famous banyan tree.

events.title: Hunter Education Commission
events.summary: Ripon appoints W.W. Hunter to review education since Wood's Despatch.
events.detail: The Commission recommended that primary education be handed to the new local boards and that private effort be encouraged with grants.
outcomes: Primary education passed to district and municipal boards.
events.yearHook: 1882: Ripon's busiest year — local self-government, Hunter Commission, press freed.

participants.role: Chaired the commission.
Appointed it.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Wood's Despatch (1854) had not spread primary education widely.
Ripon wanted local bodies to take charge of schools.
events.before: Wood's Despatch (1854) had not been fully followed; primary education was neglected.
events.after: The Commission asked that primary education be given to local boards (Ripon's new bodies) and that private schools get grants.
events.today: It is the first education commission of India.

events.title: Ilbert Bill controversy
events.summary: A bill to let Indian judges try Europeans causes a furore; white opposition forces the government to water it down (NCERT).
events.detail: The Ilbert Bill provided for the trial of British or European persons by Indians and sought equality between British and Indian judges (NCERT). Europeans in India organised a fierce campaign. When white opposition forced the government to withdraw it, Indians were enraged — the event highlighted the racial attitudes of the British (NCERT).
causes: Indian judges could not try Europeans outside the presidency towns.
course: Europeans form a Defence Association and campaign against it.
January 1884: a compromise lets Europeans demand a jury half European.
outcomes: The need for an all-India organisation of educated Indians, felt since 1880, deepened (NCERT).
Indians learnt the value of organised agitation.
facts: In 1883 there was a furore over the Ilbert Bill (NCERT).
The Ilbert Bill controversy deepened the desire for an all-India organisation (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Ilbert Bill 1883 → Congress 1885, two years later.

participants.role: Law Member who drafted the bill.
Viceroy who backed equality but gave way.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"
events.before: Indian judges could not try Europeans outside the Presidency towns.
events.after: The European protest ("white mutiny") forced a compromise: a European could ask for a jury with half Europeans. Educated Indians learnt the power of organised protest; the **Indian National Congress** came two years later (1885).
events.today: The Ilbert Bill is the classic case of racial discrimination in colonial law.

events.title: Third Anglo-Burmese War
events.summary: Dufferin deposes King Thibaw and annexes Upper Burma (1885–86).
events.detail: Fearing French influence at Mandalay and angry at a fine on a British timber company, Dufferin sent an army. King Thibaw surrendered in two weeks and was exiled to Ratnagiri; Upper Burma was annexed on 1 January 1886.
causes: Fear of French influence.
A fine on the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation.
outcomes: All of Burma became a province of British India (until 1937).
events.yearHook: Burmese wars: 1824, 1852, 1885 — the last one in the same year as the Congress.

participants.role: Viceroy who annexed Upper Burma.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: King **Thibaw** dealt with the French and fined a British timber company.
events.after: Dufferin annexed upper Burma (1 January 1886); Thibaw was exiled to **Ratnagiri**.
events.today: Thibaw Palace in Ratnagiri is a museum.

events.title: Age of Consent Act
events.summary: The age of consent for girls is raised from 10 to 12, after a campaign led by Behramji Malabari.
events.detail: The death of a child-wife, Phulmoni, in 1889 shocked many. The Act raised the age of consent to 12. Tilak opposed it as interference in Hindu customs by a foreign government.
causes: Child marriage and the death of Phulmoni (1889).
outcomes: A first legal step against child marriage; the Sarda Act followed in 1929.

pairs.left: Campaign for Age of Consent Act

events.yearHook: 1891 Age of Consent → 1929 Sarda Act.

participants.role: Viceroy who passed the Act.
Opposed the Act as foreign interference in religion.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The death of the child bride **Phulmoni** (1889) shocked people; **Behramji Malabari** campaigned.
events.after: The age of consent for girls was raised from 10 to **12**; **Tilak** opposed it as interference in religion. The **Sarda Act** (1929) set the marriage age at 14 for girls.
events.today: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (2006) sets 18 for women and 21 for men.

events.title: Indian Councils Act, 1892
events.summary: Councils get more members, some indirectly elected, and may discuss the budget.
events.detail: The Congress had demanded that Legislative Councils be made more representative and given more power (NCERT). The 1892 Act increased their size, let local bodies and universities recommend members, and allowed discussion of the budget and questions.
causes: Congress demands for more representative councils (NCERT).
outcomes: Introduced indirect election in a limited form.
Congress found it inadequate.
events.yearHook: Councils Acts: 1861, 1892, 1909.

participants.role: Viceroy when the Act was passed.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The early Congress (1885–) demanded bigger councils with elected members.
events.after: Members could discuss the budget and ask questions, and some were chosen indirectly by local bodies and universities. Moderates called it too little.
events.today: The first step towards "election" in Indian law.

events.title: Durand Line
events.summary: Mortimer Durand and Amir Abdur Rahman fix the border between British India and Afghanistan.
events.detail: The agreement drew a 2,640 km line through the Pashtun tribal lands. It became the border of Pakistan and Afghanistan after 1947.

treaties.name: Durand Line Agreement
terms: A fixed frontier through the tribal belt.
Each side not to interfere beyond it.

causes: The need for a fixed north-west frontier against Afghanistan and Russia.
events.yearHook: 1893: the Durand Line and Vivekananda at Chicago.

participants.role: Negotiated the line.
Viceroy at the time.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
outcomes: Fixed the north-west frontier of British India.
After 1947 it became the Pakistan–Afghanistan border, still disputed by Afghanistan.
events.before: The Second Afghan War (1878–80) had left Afghanistan under British control of its foreign affairs.
events.after: **Mortimer Durand** and Amir **Abdur Rahman** drew the line; the tribal belt became the **NWFP** (1901, Curzon).
events.today: Afghanistan does not accept the Durand Line as its border with Pakistan.

events.title: Vivekananda at the World Parliament of Religions, Chicago
events.summary: Swami Vivekananda's speeches at Chicago in September 1893 win the world's respect for Indian philosophy (NCERT).
events.detail: After hearing him at Chicago, the New York Herald wrote: "We feel how foolish it is to send missionaries to this learned nation" (NCERT). Vivekananda was the first Indian in modern times to re-establish Vedanta on a global scale (NCERT).
causes: Vivekananda wanted the world to know India's spiritual heritage.
outcomes: Gave Indians pride and contributed to the growing nationalism (NCERT).
The Ramakrishna Mission followed in 1897.
facts: World Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Swami Vivekananda founds the Ramakrishna Mission, stressing service to the poor (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1893 Chicago → 1897 Ramakrishna Mission.

participants.role: Spoke at the Parliament (NCERT).
His guru, whose teachings he spread (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 7
events.before: Vivekananda had travelled across India as a monk after Ramakrishna's death (1886).
events.after: His speech ("Sisters and brothers of America") made Hinduism known in the West; he founded the **Ramakrishna Mission** (1897).
events.today: 11 September 1893 is often recalled by Indian leaders in the US.

events.title: Tilak's Ganapati and Shivaji festivals
events.summary: Tilak turns Ganapati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals into public celebrations that spread nationalist ideas.
events.detail: Using religious and historical pride, Tilak brought people into politics through mass festivals. Critics said it also drew a line between Hindus and others.
causes: Tilak wanted to reach ordinary people, not only the educated.
outcomes: Built mass support for radical nationalism in Maharashtra.

alsoOn.text: Tilak starts the Shivaji festival. Gandhi and others found the Natal Indian Congress in South Africa (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Ganapati 1893, Shivaji 1895 — two years apart.

participants.role: Organised the festivals and wrote about them in Kesari.
Tilak's festival honoured him.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Tilak wanted to bring the masses into politics through religion and history.
events.after: The public **Ganapati** festival (1893) and **Shivaji** festival (1895) spread nationalism; Tilak was jailed for sedition (1897, 1908 — six years in **Mandalay**, where he wrote **Gita Rahasya**).
events.today: The public Ganeshotsav of Maharashtra and Hyderabad comes from Tilak's idea.
events.mnemonic: Lal-Bal-Pal papers "K-M-N-B": Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English) of Tilak; New India and Bande Mataram of Pal; Lajpat Rai's Punjabee.

events.title: Plague in Poona, the Chapekars and Tilak's trial
events.summary: Harsh plague measures in Poona lead the Chapekar brothers to shoot the plague commissioner; Tilak is jailed for sedition.
events.detail: Bubonic plague reached Bombay in 1896. In Poona, soldiers searched homes and forcibly removed people. On 22 June 1897 the Chapekar brothers shot the plague commissioner W.C. Rand and Lt Ayerst. Tilak, who had criticised the measures in Kesari, was sentenced to 18 months for sedition.
causes: Brutal plague searches by soldiers in Poona homes.
The famine of 1896–97.
outcomes: Tilak became a national hero; "Lokmanya".
The first major political assassination of the period.
events.yearHook: Plague 1896, murder and Tilak's trial 1897.

participants.role: Shot Rand and Ayerst; later hanged.
Jailed for sedition for his articles in Kesari.
Viceroy at the time.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Plague struck Poona; officer **W. C. Rand** used soldiers to search homes and remove the sick.
events.after: The **Chapekar brothers** shot Rand and Lt. Ayerst (22 June 1897) — the first political murder of a British officer in India. Tilak was jailed for 18 months for his articles.
events.today: Damodar and Balkrishna Chapekar are remembered in Pune (Chinchwad).

events.title: Birsa Munda's Ulgulan
events.summary: In December 1899 Birsa Munda's followers rise against dikus, missionaries and the British, to set up a Munda Raj (NCERT).
events.detail:
The land policies of the British were destroying the Mundas' traditional land system, landlords and moneylenders were taking over their land, and missionaries were criticising their culture (NCERT). Birsa urged his followers to destroy "Ravana" (dikus and the Europeans) and set up a kingdom under his leadership (NCERT).

His followers attacked police stations and churches and raided the property of moneylenders and zamindars, raising the white flag of Birsa Raj (NCERT). In 1900 Birsa died of cholera and the movement faded out (NCERT).
causes: British land policies destroyed the traditional Munda land system (khuntkatti) (NCERT).
Landlords and moneylenders took over Munda land (NCERT).
Missionaries criticised Munda culture (NCERT).
Forced labour (beth begari) for zamindars.
course: 1895: Birsa urges the Mundas to recover their glorious past (NCERT).
1895: he is arrested and jailed for two years (NCERT).
1897: released, he tours villages gathering support (NCERT).
December 1899: followers attack police stations, churches and moneylenders (NCERT).
1900: Birsa is captured and dies of cholera in Ranchi jail (NCERT).
losses: Hundreds of Mundas killed or jailed.
outcomes: Forced the government to pass laws so that tribal land could not easily be taken by dikus — the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 (NCERT).
Showed again that tribal people could protest against injustice (NCERT).
facts: Birsa was arrested in 1895 and released in 1897 (NCERT).
In 1900 Birsa died of cholera (NCERT).
His followers raised the white flag of Birsa Raj (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Birsa Munda calls the Mundas to recover their golden past; he is arrested and jailed for two years (NCERT).
Birsa Munda is released and tours the villages (NCERT).
Birsa Munda dies of cholera in Ranchi jail (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1899–1900: Ulgulan ("great tumult"); Birsa dies in Ranchi jail, 9 June 1900, aged 25.

participants.role: Led the movement; arrested, then died in jail of cholera (NCERT).
Viceroy at the time.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 4 "Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age"
events.before: Mundas lost their land (khuntkatti) to outsiders (dikus) and were forced into begar (unpaid labour); missionaries and landlords pressed them.
events.after: The **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act** (1908) protected Munda land.
events.today: His birthday, **15 November**, is **Janjatiya Gaurav Divas**; Jharkhand was formed on that day (2000).

events.title: Servants of India Society; Gokhale presides at Benares
events.summary: G.K. Gokhale founds the Servants of India Society to train selfless workers for the nation.
events.detail: Members took vows of poverty and service. The same year Gokhale presided over the Benares session of the Congress, which condemned the partition of Bengal.
causes: Gokhale wanted trained, full-time workers for public life.
outcomes: Members worked in famine relief, education and labour welfare.
events.yearHook: 1905: Bengal partitioned and Gokhale's society founded.

participants.role: Founded the society and presided over the Benares Congress.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Gokhale, the leading Moderate, wanted trained public workers.
events.after: The Servants of India Society trained volunteers for social service; Gokhale presided over the **Benares Congress** (1905), which backed swadeshi in Bengal.
events.today: The Society (Pune) still runs; Gandhi called Gokhale his political guru.

events.title: First Rampa rebellion under Tammandora
events.summary: The hill people (Koyas and Konda Doras) of the Rampa country in the Godavari Agency rise (1879–80) against the local mansabdar, police and new excise and forest rules. The British need troops and about a year to crush it.
events.detail:
Leaders: **Tammandora** (Tammana Dora) and **Chandrayya**. Causes: a hated **mansabdar** (local revenue chief) raising rents, new **toddy (excise)** rules that stopped the tribals tapping their own palms, and forest rules limiting **podu** (shifting) cultivation and grazing.

Police stations were attacked and the revolt spread across the hill tracts of the Godavari Agency.
events.source: Sarojini Regani, Highlights of the Freedom Movement in Andhra Pradesh; Telugu Akademi, Andhra Pradesh History; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1879: 43 years before Alluri's rebellion (1922) in the same hills.
events.before: The **Agency** tracts of the Godavari and Visakhapatnam hills had been ruled lightly through local chiefs.
events.after: The same grievances — forest laws, forced labour, outsiders — led to **Alluri Sitarama Raju**'s Rampa rebellion (1922–24).
events.today: The Fifth Schedule of the Constitution (Scheduled Areas) and the PESA Act (1996) grew out of the old "Agency" idea.
events.mnemonic: Two Rampa revolts "79 and 22": Tammandora (1879) and Alluri (1922–24).

events.title: Mayo: financial decentralisation, the first census, and his assassination
events.summary: Viceroy Mayo (1869–72) gives the provinces fixed grants to run police, jails, education and roads (financial decentralisation, 1870) and holds the first census (1872, not taken at the same time everywhere). He is stabbed to death by a convict, Sher Ali, while visiting the Andaman Islands (1872).
events.detail:
Mayo also founded the **Mayo College** at Ajmer (1875) for the sons of princes and set up a **Department of Agriculture and Commerce**. He is the only Viceroy killed in office.

The first **synchronous** census (all at once) came in **1881** under Ripon, with W. C. Plowden as Census Commissioner.
events.source: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India; NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1872: 14 years after Crown rule (1858); the first all-India census at one time comes nine years later (1881).
events.before: **Lawrence** (1864–69) had followed "masterly inactivity" towards Afghanistan; provincial finances were controlled from Calcutta.
events.after: **Ripon** (1880–84) built on financial decentralisation with local self-government (1882).
events.today: India's next census (2027) will be the first digital one and will count caste.
events.mnemonic: Census "72 and 81": Mayo's first count (1872), Ripon's first regular census (1881); then every ten years until 2011.

events.title: Darul Uloom Deoband founded
events.summary: Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi found the Darul Uloom at Deoband (Saharanpur, UP) in 1866 to train Muslim scholars in traditional Islamic learning, after the defeat of 1857.
events.detail:
Two streams of Muslim reform: **Deoband** (traditional, anti-British, later supported the Congress; **Mahmud-ul-Hasan**, **Hussain Ahmad Madani**) and **Aligarh** (modern Western education, loyal to the British; Sayyid Ahmad Khan). Earlier came the **Wahabi** movement of **Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli** (1820s–1870s).

Other community reform: Parsis — **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha** (1851, Naoroji, Banerji); Sikhs — **Singh Sabha** (Amritsar, 1873) and later the **Akali** movement (1920s, Gurdwara Act 1925).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.5 and 8; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1866: nine years after 1857; nine years before Aligarh (1875).
events.before: The revolt of 1857 had ended the Mughal throne; Muslim scholars feared for their faith and learning.
events.after: Deoband's scholars backed the **Khilafat** movement (1919–24) and the Congress against partition.
events.today: Darul Uloom Deoband is one of the largest Islamic seminaries in the world.
events.mnemonic: Muslim reform "W-D-A-A": Wahabi (1820s), Deoband (1866), Aligarh (1875), Ahmadiya (1889).

events.title: Prarthana Samaj founded in Bombay
events.summary: Inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen's visit, Dr Atmaram Pandurang founds the Prarthana Samaj (prayer society) in Bombay (1867). M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar make it the main reform body of western India.
events.detail:
It worked for women's education, widow remarriage, raising the age of marriage and against caste, drawing on the Marathi **bhakti** saints (Tukaram, Namdev). Ranade also founded the **Widow Remarriage Association** (1861), the **Deccan Education Society** (1884) and the **Indian National Social Conference** (1887).

Women reformers of western India: **Pandita Ramabai** (Arya Mahila Samaj, Sharada Sadan), **Tarabai Shinde** (Stri Purush Tulana, 1882), **Savitribai Phule** (first girls' school with Jyotirao, Pune, 1848), **D. K. Karve** (widows' home, SNDT Women's University, 1916).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.5 and 8; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1867: 39 years after the Brahmo Sabha (1828); 8 years before the Arya Samaj (1875).
events.before: The **Paramahansa Mandali** (1849) had met secretly in Bombay against caste.
events.after: **Veeresalingam** founded the first Prarthana Samaj in Andhra at Rajahmundry (1878).
events.today: SNDT Women's University (Mumbai) and the Deccan Education Society (Fergusson College) still run.
events.mnemonic: Reform bodies by year "B-P-A-T-R" = 1828-1867-1875-1875-1897: Brahmo, Prarthana, Arya, Theosophical (New York), Ramakrishna Mission.

events.title: Vivekananda founds the Ramakrishna Mission
events.summary: Back from America, Swami Vivekananda founds the Ramakrishna Mission (1 May 1897) to serve the poor, sick and ignorant as a form of worshipping God ("service to man is service to God").
events.detail:
**Ramakrishna Paramahamsa** (1836–1886), a priest at Dakshineswar, taught that all religions lead to the same God. His disciple **Narendranath Datta** (Vivekananda) took his message to the world at the **Chicago Parliament of Religions** (11 September 1893).

The Mission's headquarters is at **Belur Math** (1898–99), near Kolkata; it runs schools, hospitals and relief work.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.5 and 8; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1897: four years after Chicago (1893); Vivekananda dies in 1902, aged 39.
events.before: The Brahmo and Arya Samajs had reformed Hinduism by rejecting idols; Ramakrishna accepted every form of worship.
events.after: Vivekananda inspired nationalists like **Aurobindo**, **Tilak** and **Subhas Bose**; Sister **Nivedita** (Margaret Noble) worked in Calcutta.
events.today: His birthday, 12 January, is **National Youth Day**; the Vivekananda Rock Memorial stands at Kanyakumari.

events.title: Gandhi in South Africa: the birth of satyagraha
events.summary: Gandhi, a young lawyer, goes to South Africa (1893) for a case. Thrown off a first-class train at Pietermaritzburg for being Indian, he stays 21 years and develops satyagraha — non-violent resistance to unjust laws.
events.detail:
Steps: **Natal Indian Congress** (1894); the paper **Indian Opinion** (1903); **Phoenix Settlement** (1904, near Durban); the first **satyagraha** against the "Black Act" (Asiatic registration, 1906); **Tolstoy Farm** (1910, near Johannesburg); the great march of 1913 against the £3 tax and the ruling that Hindu and Muslim marriages were invalid. The **Indian Relief Act** (1914) met many demands.

Influences: **Tolstoy** (The Kingdom of God is Within You), **Ruskin** (Unto This Last — "Sarvodaya"), **Thoreau** (Civil Disobedience), the Gita and Jain ideas of ahimsa.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.9; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1893: the same year as Vivekananda's Chicago speech (1893). Gandhi returns to India in 1915.
events.before: Gandhi (born 1869, Porbandar) studied law in London (1888–91) and failed to build a practice in Bombay.
events.after: He came back in **January 1915** with a method and a name; **Gokhale** became his political guru.
events.today: Pietermaritzburg station has a plaque; 9 January (his return) is Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.
events.mnemonic: South Africa "N-I-P-S-T-R" (1894–1914): Natal Congress, Indian Opinion, Phoenix, Satyagraha (1906), Tolstoy Farm, Relief Act.
